extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century periodical readers; theatre-goers, essayists, critics and general public
extracted.subtask_description: Short, opinionated periodical essays and theatrical/social criticism aimed at a broad literate public, advising on manners, rhetoric, and what merits praise in theatre and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest amplification in retelling stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story has been told with entertaining circumstances, to tell it over again with particulars that destroy the jest but give light into the truth is an amiable sort of veracity, because it proceeds from the love of truth even in frivolous occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and value truthful elaboration that clarifies facts even if it lessens entertainment value; such ‘honest amendments’ mark a sincere friend or reliable narrator and may be preferable when the correction does no harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose lies born of arrogance or malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lies which are told out of arrogance and ostentation a man should detect in his own defence; lies which are told out of malice he should expose, both for his own sake and that of the rest of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing about deception, distinguish motive: correct vanity-driven falsehoods to avoid being triumphed over; expose malicious falsehoods as public harms that deserve rebuttal and censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate officious falsehoods that do good
rubrics_metrics.description: The officious Liar...is to be excused, because it does some Man good, and no Man hurt; the man who lies into good humour may be half excusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In characterisation and social practice, permit small, benevolent deceptions that reconcile, cheer, or repair relationships—so long as they cause no harm—recognizing a moral nuance in truth-telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indirect flattery and conciliatory speech
rubrics_metrics.description: He will tell one Beauty she was commended by another...by these indirect offices he reconciles parties, makes people meet and crack a bottle, turns railing into mutual kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rhetorical or narrative technique, employ indirect praise and tactful misrepresentation to create reconciliations and social comedy; this is a legitimate device for plotting, dialogue, and social maneuvering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical merit: 'shining Thought' and 'uncommon Grace'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trunk-maker smites when 'any shining Thought is expressed in the Poet, or any uncommon Grace appears in the Actor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theatre criticism and dramatic writing, prioritize recognisable, striking ideas (shining thoughts) in the script and graceful, distinguished performance qualities in actors as primary grounds for applause and acclaim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and leadership of audience response
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been observed, his Blow is so well timed, that the most judicious Critick could never except against it...the Trunk-maker presides over their Heads like the Director of a Consort, in order to awaken their Attention, and beat time to their Applauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience reaction is partly cultivated: effective critics or stage managers can lead and time applause to focus attention. Writers and performers should be aware of pacing and cues that invite timely audience approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of applause (not mere 'brutum fulmen')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Actors do not value themselves upon the Clap, but regard it as a meer Brutum fulmen, or empty Noise, when it has not the Sound of the Oaken Plant in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine acclaim from hollow clapping; in assessing performance or writing, give weight to praise that is informed and authoritative rather than spontaneous but uninformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic selection: judgment informed by literary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: None preferred to the post who has not given convincing proofs both of a sound Judgment and a strong Arm, and who could not, upon Occasion, either knock down an Ox, or write a Comment upon Horace's Art of Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirically expressed, this prescribes that a public arbiter of taste combine solid critical judgement (knowledge of poetic/artistic standards like Horace) with the moral authority to sway audiences; in practice, choose critics on the basis of literary competence and demonstrable influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical clarity: do not mistake licentiousness for freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Their Pretension to be Free-thinkers...they disdain Deduction, Coherence, Consistency, and all the Rules of Reason...Licentiousness is not Freedom; a Prejudice towards Atheism is not Impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing polemic or philosophical prose, preserve logical coherence, consistency, and respect for reason; avoid conflating boldness or licence in speech with true intellectual freedom—argument should be principled, not merely provocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of married behavior: civility and benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be civil at least is not beneath the Character of a Gentleman...voluntary Civility, and the Greatness of Soul that is conspicuous in Benevolence without immediate Obligations...would make Marriage more easy and comfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social and character writing, depict healthy conjugal relations through small civilities, tenderness, and voluntary benevolence rather than affectation of hardness; such particulars create believable, admirable domestic characters and moral argumentation.
